{{short description|Statistical test for equality of variances}}
The '''Brown–Forsythe test''' is a [[statistical test]] for the equality of group variances based on performing an [[Analysis of Variance]] (ANOVA) on a [[Data transformation (statistics)|transformation]] of the [[response variable]]. When a [[one-way ANOVA]] is performed, samples are assumed to have been drawn from distributions with equal [[variance]]. If this assumption is not valid, the resulting [[F-test|''F''-test]] is invalid. The Brown–Forsythe [[test statistic]] is the F statistic resulting from an ordinary one-way analysis of variance on the absolute deviations of the groups or treatments data  from their individual medians.<ref name=plothov>{{cite web |title=plot.hov function {{!}} R Documentation |url=https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/HH/versions/3.1-39/topics/plot.hov |website=www.rdocumentation.org |publisher=DataCamp}}</ref>

==Transformation==
The transformed response variable is constructed to measure the [[statistical dispersion|spread]] in each group. Let

: <math>
z_{ij}=\left\vert y_{ij} - \tilde{y}_j \right\vert
</math>

where <math>\tilde{y}_j</math> is the [[median]] of group ''j''.  The Brown–Forsythe test statistic is the model ''F'' statistic from a one way ANOVA on ''z<sub>ij</sub>'':

: <math>F = \frac{(N-p)}{(p-1)} \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{p} n_j (\tilde{z}_{\cdot j}-\tilde{z}_{\cdot\cdot})^2} {\sum_{j=1}^{p}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j} (z_{ij}-\tilde{z}_{\cdot j})^2}</math>

where ''p'' is the number of groups, ''n<sub>j</sub>'' is the number of observations in group ''j'', and ''N'' is the total number of observations. Also <math>\tilde{z}_{\cdot j}</math> are the group means of the <math>z_{ij}</math> and <math>\tilde{z}_{\cdot\cdot}</math> is the overall mean of the <math>z_{ij}</math>.  This ''F''-statistic follows the [[F-distribution|''F''-distribution]] with degrees of freedom <math>d_1=p-1</math> and <math>d_2=N-p</math> under the null hypothesis.

If the variances are indeed heterogeneous, techniques that allow for this (such as the [[Welch one-way ANOVA]]) may be used instead of the usual ANOVA.

Good, noting that the deviations are linearly dependent, has modified the test so as to drop the redundant deviations.<ref name=Good2005>{{cite book |last=Good|first=P. I.|author-link=Phillip Good |title=Permutation, Parametric, and Bootstrap Tests of Hypotheses |edition=3rd |location=New York |publisher=Springer |year=2005 }}</ref>

==Comparison with Levene's test==
[[Levene's test]] uses the mean instead of the median. Although the optimal choice depends on the underlying distribution, the definition based on the median is recommended as the choice that provides good [[Robust statistics|robustness]] against many types of non-normal data while retaining good [[statistical power]].<ref name=Derrick2018>{{cite journal|last1=Derrick|first1=B|last2=Ruck|first2=A| last3=Toher|first3=D|last4=White|first4=P|title=Tests for equality of variances between two samples which contain both paired observations and independent observations |journal=Journal of Applied Quantitative Methods |date=2018|volume=13|issue=2|pages=36–47| url=http://jaqm.ro/issues/volume-13,issue-2/pdfs/3_BE_AN_DE_PA_.pdf}}</ref>
If one has knowledge of the underlying distribution of the data, this may indicate using one of the other choices. Brown and Forsythe<ref name=BrownForsythe1974>{{cite journal |last1=Brown |first1=Morton B. |last2=Forsythe |first2=Alan B. |year=1974 |title=Robust tests for the equality of variances |journal=[[Journal of the American Statistical Association]] |volume=69 |issue=346|pages=364–367 |doi=10.1080/01621459.1974.10482955 |jstor=2285659}}</ref> performed [[Monte Carlo method|Monte Carlo]] studies that indicated that using the [[trimmed mean]] performed best when the underlying data followed a [[Cauchy distribution]] (a [[heavy-tailed]] distribution) and the median performed best when the underlying data followed a [[Chi-squared distribution|χ<sup>2</sup> distribution]] with four degrees of freedom (a sharply [[skewness|skewed distribution]]). Using the mean provided the best power for symmetric, moderate-tailed, distributions. O'Brien tested several ways of using the traditional analysis of variance to test heterogeneity of spread in [[factorial]] designs with equal or unequal sample sizes. The jackknife pseudovalues of s<sup>2</sup> and the absolute deviations from the cell median are shown to be robust and relatively powerful.<ref name="O'Brien1978">{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1007/BF02293643| title = Robust techniques for testing heterogeneity of variance effects in factorial designs| journal = [[Psychometrika]]| volume = 43| issue = 3| pages = 327–342| year = 1978| last1 = O'Brien | first1 = R. G. }}</ref>
